stories.headline: Update: Vance Arrives in Switzerland as Iran Closes Strait of Hormuz, Complicating Peace Talks
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance arrived in Switzerland on Sunday to join special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner for technical-level negotiations with Iran, aimed at building on the recently signed memorandum of understanding to end hostilities. The talks, originally scheduled for Friday, were delayed after Iran's armed forces announced they were closing the Strait of Hormuz — just three days after it had reopened — citing continued Israeli strikes on Hezbollah in Lebanon as violations of the interim ceasefire deal.

Iran's top military command said the waterway closure was a direct response to Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon that it said violated the U.S.-Iran agreement. Vance, speaking on Fox News before departing, said he had seen no evidence that Iran had actually blocked the strait, and the U.S. disputed Iran's claim outright. Pakistan, one of the key mediators, confirmed that talks would proceed in Switzerland on Sunday, with Islamabad sending its prime minister and military chief to participate.

President Trump, responding on Truth Social, threatened to impose tolls on the Strait of Hormuz if a permanent deal is not completed within 60 days. Trump also suggested that Iran retaining some missile capability may be acceptable, striking a notably different tone from the administration's earlier justifications for military action. He separately lashed out at critics of the MOU, calling Democratic opponents "Radical Left fools."

The episode represents the first significant crisis to emerge since the MOU was signed, and it underscores the fragility of the peace framework. Republicans are divided on the deal, with some praising progress on the nuclear file while others warn the agreement grants Tehran billions in economic relief without enforceable inspection mechanisms. Democrats have largely argued the war produced no concrete gains while inflicting economic pain on American consumers through energy price disruptions.

stories.headline: Update: Keir Starmer Expected to Resign as UK Prime Minister, Set Exit Timetable
stories.summary:
Britain's Observer newspaper reported that Prime Minister Keir Starmer is expected to announce his resignation on Monday and set out a timetable for an orderly departure, a development that would end his tenure less than two years after Labour's landslide election victory. A government source pushed back, telling Reuters that Starmer remained focused on governing, but a cabinet ally separately acknowledged the prime minister was weighing "political realities."

UK Business Secretary Peter Kyle said publicly that Starmer is reflecting on those realities, a notably candid admission that added weight to the resignation reports. The political pressure on Starmer has intensified following Andy Burnham's return to Parliament after winning a by-election, positioning the Greater Manchester mayor as a prominent leadership challenger.

Starmer's premiership has been battered by persistently low approval ratings, internal party tensions, and difficult economic conditions. His government faced criticism from both the left — over perceived moderation on key Labour policy commitments — and from centrists concerned about electoral vulnerabilities heading toward the next general election.

If confirmed, Starmer's departure would trigger a Labour leadership contest at a critical moment for British politics, with the opposition Conservatives still rebuilding and Reform UK gaining ground in polls. The transition would mark a significant moment for the UK's governing coalition and its relationships with European partners and the United States.

stories.headline: Update: Trump-Meloni Feud Deepens as Italy Cancels U.S. Diplomatic Visit
stories.summary:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni publicly told President Trump to "focus on your own popularity" in a pointed Instagram statement on Saturday, escalating a public dispute that has strained one of Trump's previously closest European relationships. Trump had renewed his attack on Meloni, accusing her of requesting a photo with him "over and over" at the G7 summit in France and claiming she had caused a "great logistical inconvenience" by denying U.S. forces access to Italian air facilities during military operations against Iran.

Meloni rejected both claims, saying Italian base access is governed by existing agreements "that cannot be violated as long as I am prime minister," and that Trump's attacks were "constant, unprovoked" and "senseless." She noted pointedly that being Trump's friend had not helped her domestic approval ratings. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani subsequently cancelled a planned visit to Washington scheduled for early next week.

The confrontation has drawn support for Meloni from across Italy's political spectrum, including from opposition parties, and reflects growing European frustration with Trump's conduct toward allied governments. Italy was the sole European nation to send its leader to Trump's inauguration in January 2025, and Meloni had cultivated a close personal relationship with the American president built on shared right-nationalist political affinities.

The rift traces in part to Italy's refusal to allow U.S. use of its bases during the Iran war, which Trump and Italian officials characterize very differently. The public exchange marks a significant deterioration in transatlantic relations at a moment when the U.S. is simultaneously negotiating a fragile peace framework in the Middle East and pressing NATO allies on defense spending commitments.

stories.headline: Colombia Presidential Runoff Pits Leftist Negotiator Against Trump-Backed Security Hardliner
stories.summary:
Colombians head to the polls Sunday in a high-stakes presidential runoff that presents starkly contrasting visions for addressing the country's escalating internal conflict. Left-wing senator Iván Cepeda, the architect of outgoing President Gustavo Petro's "total peace" strategy of negotiating with armed groups, faces conservative businessman Abelardo de la Espriella — known as El Tigre — who has promised mass incarceration, military crackdowns, and an end to all negotiations with cartels and guerrilla factions.

The election comes as illegal armed groups, including FARC dissident factions, the ELN, and the Clan del Golfo, have roughly doubled their membership over the last five years, driving a reported 300 percent increase in forced displacement between 2024 and 2025. Tens of thousands of Colombians have been displaced by renewed fighting near the Venezuelan border, and the campaign itself was marked by the assassination of a presidential candidate, along with widespread homicides, kidnappings, and bombings.

De la Espriella, who holds U.S. citizenship and has received Donald Trump's endorsement, has promised ten mega-prisons and a military offensive against armed groups, saying any criminal who does not surrender "will be taken down." Critics of Cepeda's approach argue that the Petro government's negotiation strategy allowed armed groups to exploit ceasefire periods to expand territorial control; supporters say it prevented greater bloodshed.

The outcome will have significant implications for U.S.-Colombia relations, drug trafficking interdiction cooperation, and the future of the 2016 peace agreement that disarmed thousands of FARC fighters. Colombia remains the world's leading cocaine producer, and the stability of its government is closely watched across Latin America and in Washington.
